text: On June eighth, twenty twenty-three, lightning hit a forest in eastern Kazakhstan. The fire burned sixty thousand hectares, and fifteen people died. Every year, Kazakhstan's steppe and forests burn.
But Kazakhstan is huge: two point seven million square kilometers. Rangers can't watch everywhere. Every evening, they have to guess: where do we look tomorrow?

So I built Saqshy. It means guardian in Kazakh. Every evening, it takes NASA satellite fire detections and weather for thirteen hundred squares across the whole country, and ranks them by tomorrow's fire risk. This is a real evening, April twenty-ninth, twenty twenty-five, from a season the model never saw. The red squares are its riskiest ten percent. The next day, satellites saw fires in eighty-two squares. Fifty-six of them were inside Saqshy's red zone. The Canadian Fire Weather Index caught just one, because it pointed at the hot southern deserts, where there's little to burn. Each district then gets a short alert in Kazakh or Russian.

I trained gradient-boosted trees on 2012 to 2022, and tested them on every day of three new fire seasons. If rangers watch only ten percent of the country, Saqshy's map holds sixty-nine percent of tomorrow's fires. Watching last week's fires gets sixty-two. The weather indices get eleven.

It's not magic. Saqshy missed the start of the Abai fire, because lightning leaves no trace in yesterday's data. But the next evening, that fire was in its top one percent. Next, I'll add lightning forecasts, and send alerts to rangers and farmers next spring. Saqshy: see the fire before it spreads.
